title.narrative: ILO, 2022-2025, Decent Work and Labour Rights in Southern Africa
ILO, 2022-2025, Decent Work and Labour Rights in Southern Africa

description.narrative: Det aktuella projektet har arbetande fattiga unga, män och kvinnor som målgrupp. Det bygger på ett starkt partnerskap mellan International Labour Organisation (ILO), Southern African Development Community (SADC) och dess medlemsländer, och viktiga intressenter såsom The Southern African Trade Union Coordination Council (SATUCC) och SADC Private Sector Forum (SPSF). Projektet kommer att arbeta på två nivåer med syftet att stärka SADC-sekretariatets kapacitet att förespråka uppskalning av systeminsatser; föreslå och främja effektiva policyförändringar i dess medlemsländer samt att driva på långsiktiga och hållbara förbättringar för utsatta unga, kvinnor och män i byggnadssektorn (sub-regional nivå). Dessutom kommer nationella projekt att genomföras liksom samarbete med nationella regeringar, privata aktörer, fackföreningar och arbetsgivarorganisationer i Moçambique, Zimbabwe och Sydafrika för att ta itu med viktiga systembegränsningar i en sektor där den stora majoriteten arbetskraft är lågavlönad och där bristande säkerhet och informell anställning är rådande. De tre föreslagna länderna har identifierats och valts ut på grund av deras snabbt växande byggnadssektorer, underskott i anständiga arbetsvillkor liksom på grund av existerande erfarenheter och relationer med nyckelpartners och pågående relaterade utvecklingsinsatser.

Targeting the working poor young, men and women, and the micro, small and medium sized enterprises (MSMEs) of the building construction sector that employ a majority of the labour force in the Southern Africa sub-region, the Project builds on an already strong partnership between International Labour Organisation (ILO), Southern African Development Community (SADC) and its member states, and vital stakeholders such as Southern African Trade Union Coordination Council (SATUCC) and SADC Private Sector Forum (SPSF). Adopting a market systems development approach, the Project will work on two levels aimed to strengthen the capacity of the SADC Secretariat to advocate for scaling-up systemic interventions; propose and promote effective policy change across its member states, and drive long-term and sustainable improvements for vulnerable female and male labourers in the building-construction sector (sub-regional level); and to implement national projects and engage with national governments, private sector actors, trade unions and employers organisations in Mozambique, Zimbabwe and South Africa by addressing key systemic constraints in the sector in which the vast majority of workers are locked in low wage, inadequate safety and informal employment (see footnote). The three suggested countries have been identified and selected due to their growing construction sectors, decent work deficits as well as experiences and relationships with key partners and ongoing related interventions.

The project objective is to contribute to improved labour rights in the building-construction sector in the Southern Africa Development Community. The project, which will be implemented using a systemic approach to decent work and will work at the sub-regional level (Outcome 1) as well as in three countries: South Africa, Mozambique and Zimbabwe (Outcome 2).
The project will aim to improve labour rights through targeting interventions that provide benefit to the working poor and young women and men and the micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) that employ them. These target groups include the workers who are most likely to have few labour rights - including poor wages, occupational safety and health, contract stability and informality and the MSMEs, who disproportionately struggle to provide decent work to their employees relative to larger contractors.
As the project will be grounded in a systemic approach to decent work, it will strive to benefit the target groups in long-term sustainable way that can reach scale. It will do this by working through key project partners, including the South African Development Community (SADC), regional and national employers associations and trade unions, SADC member government bodies and the private sector.

The 2024 report summarizes progress done so far. In summary, some activities/outputs have recorded more progress than others. Here is summary of the progress under each outcome and output.
Under Outcome 1, the project have country level activities that targets enterprises to help them improve working conditions and enhance labour productivity in the construction market systems of Mozambique, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. The project targets trade unions, social protection agencies, tendering/procurement authorities, Business Service Developers (BDS) and labour inspectorates in the target countries.
Strengthened Union Representation:
Project reports that enterprises in Mozambique, South Africa, and Zimbabwe are working to improve working conditions and enhance labour productivity in the construction market systems. In Mozambique, the apex trade union CONSILMO is finalizing an advocacy strategy for construction workers. In South Africa, two construction sector trade unions, BCAWU and NUM, have developed strategies for more structured advocacy for workers' rights, including a labour rights handbook. In Zimbabwe, the construction sector trade union ZCATWU has developed an advocacy strategy and an OSH manual.
Expanded Social Protection Mechanims:
A comprehensive analysis of social protection needs for workers in Zimbabwe's construction sector has been conducted, which led to evidence-based recommendations for a more responsive social protection scheme. However, there have been delays in updating and developing small works and employment contracts to integrate decent work elements. In Zimbabwe, a partnership with the Ministry of Public Works aims to develop the Construction Contractor Bill and standardize contracts. In South Africa, a partnership with the Waterberg Municipality is being established to train MSMEs and certify SMEs in handling fly ash.
Integration of Decent Work in Procurement
The project is also working on revising tendering processes to integrate decent work elements in the procurement of construction services, though this is behind schedule. In Zimbabwe, the development of the Construction Contractor Bill and standardization of contracts are ongoing. In South Africa, the partnership with Waterberg Municipality aims to improve MSMEs' working conditions and productivity.
Enhanced Business Development Services
To enhance business development support services and promote decent work standards, partnerships have been established with five Business Development Service (BDS) Providers in the pilot countries. These providers are training and mentoring MSMEs to improve working conditions and compliance with labour laws. The capacity of 31 Business Development Services Practitioners from 17 BDS providers has been enhanced. To date, 93 small and medium enterprises employing an estimated 4,845 workers have been trained and are currently receiving mentorship.
Improved Access to Worker Protection and Labour Inspection
In Zimbabwe, an agreement with the National Social Security Agency (NSSA) and discussions with Old Mutual aim to design and pilot workers insurance schemes for SMEs. Labour inspection mechanisms are being developed to reach vulnerable workers in the construction sector. In Mozambique, a strategic approach to promoting labour rights compliance has been introduced but is on hold due to political factors. In South Africa, 28 Labour Inspectors have been trained on promoting labour law compliance. In Zimbabwe, a strategic compliance approach and an electronic system for managing labour rights violations have been introduced.
Outcome 2: SADC adopts strategies to improve labor rights for women and youth, based on evidence-based solutions.
A comparative analysis study is currently underway to assess maternity protection and gender equity practices in the construction sector in Mozambique, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and the Seychelles. This analysis aims to evaluate existing policies and identify good practices, which will be shared with the wider SADC member states. Additionally, a study exploring the link between decent work and enterprise productivity is in progress. This research seeks to establish how good labour practices and a conducive work environment lead to increased productivity, higher efficiency, and overall competitiveness. The project is also organizing a Dialogue on decent work and Labour Productivity among Trade Unions from Mozambique, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, which will take place in the next reporting cycle. The findings from these studies will be deliberated on at the SADC ministerial level once available and the recommendations will be binding to all SADC member states once approved.
